title: Claude Caught a Security Risk I Didn't Even Think About
central_idea: Claude proactively flagged exposed API keys in the environment instead of silently using them, forcing a better architectural decision.
audience: Developers and builders who use AI coding assistants and care about security hygiene
hook_candidates: I asked Claude to build a safe demo with no real API keys — then Claude found my real API keys and stopped everything.
Most AI tools would have just used the credentials sitting in your environment. Claude didn't.
I thought I was being careful. Claude was being more careful than me.

title: How to Keep API Keys Safe in a Local Chatbot Demo
central_idea: When building a browser-facing chatbot demo, API keys must live server-side only — never in client JavaScript — even for a local recording.
audience: Developers building demos or prototypes who may not have considered client-side key exposure
hook_candidates: If your API key is in your frontend JavaScript, anyone watching your screen recording can steal it.
Here's the one rule for demo chatbots: the API key never leaves the server.
A DevTools tab or a network inspector is all it takes to expose a raw API key in client-side code.

title: I Built a Bilingual Personal-Brand Chatbot in One Session
central_idea: Starting from a safe mock demo and one security pivot, Mohammad ended up with a working local bilingual AI assistant ready for video.
audience: Creators and indie builders interested in shipping personal-brand tools quickly with AI assistance
hook_candidates: I went from 'mock demo only' to a real bilingual AI chatbot in a single session — here's what happened in between.
Ask it a question in English, it answers in English. Ask in Arabic, it answers in Arabic. Built this in one sitting.
The goal was a simple fake demo for a video. I ended up with something actually worth shipping.
